newsitem.title: USA: U.S. election producing huge yawn among voters.
newsitem.headline: U.S. election producing huge yawn among voters.

text.p: Bob Dole, ever hopeful, says that once the professional baseball playoffs end later this month, Americans will really zero in on the November 5 U.S. presidential election -- and he will overhaul Bill Clinton.
"The American people are begining to focus on the campaign," Dole said this week while campaigning outside Chicago. They will really tune in after the baseball championships conclude, he added.
That is an old American folk saying -- the campaign only starts after the World Series ends -- but it has always been dubious and, this year especially, Dole should be so lucky.
The evidence suggests many Americans just aren't interested in the Republican nominee and his battle to oust the incumbent Democratic president.

Dole, after all, had already said voter interest would pick up after he quit the Senate last May, foresaking a 35-year Washington career to campaign full-time. He said it again after the Labour Day holiday in early September brought people back to reality from summer vacations.
But apathy still seems to prevail, and pollsters see a possibility of the lowest voter turnout ever for a U.S. presidential election.
Turnout hit a new low of about half of all eligible voters In 1988. It rose a bit in 1992, but that race was spiced up by the novelty of a strong new third-force candidate, Ross Perot.
Polls this year show a disinterested electorate bored by the candidates, their constant barrage of television "infomercial" campaign ads and uninspiring debates.
Larry Hugick of Princeton Research Survey Associates in New Jersey sums up: "It's a boring campaign."
"It's been hard to make a compelling case" to attract press attention, Hugick said, although he does not blame the press. "There hasn't been much to cover," he concluded.

Hugick found that the voters both parties are trying hardest to attract are the most tuned-out: younger, mainly moderate types who call themselves independent and comprise the half of the electorate between ages 18 and 44.
Bill Moyers, who was President Lyndon Johnson's press secretary and now makes public television documentaries, said politics is now a spectator sport with little worth watching.
"People have tuned out this election, they are not connecting," Moyers said. "Dole is not resonating and Clinton is not addressing the issues."

A Pew Research Centre survey found that only 24 percent of eligible voters said they are following the election very closely, a sharp decline from 42 percent who said they were doing so four years ago. Dole's running mate, Jack Kemp, is unknown to 40 percent of those surveyed.

The television audience for the first presidential debate last Sunday in Hartford, Connecticut fell to the lowest level in their 36-year history, down about 20 percent from 1992 when Perot's participation sparked interest.

The Nielsen ratings for the debate found that only 32 percent of U.S. homes tuned in, down from 38 percent in 1992. Nielsen, which rates television audiences, said the highest-rated televised debate was the first one in 1960 between John Kennedy and Richard Nixon.
This year the yawner race has become the butt of late night television comedy.

"Late Show" host David Letterman this week offered 10 suggestions for tweaking interest in next week's second and last debate in San Diego. Among them was: "give the candidates a choice of five podiums, one of which will explode."
